Electron Self-Energy and Generalized Drude Formula
for Infrared Conductivity of Metals

Philip B. Allen Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, State University of New York, Stony Brook, NY 11794-3800
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Götze and Wölfle (GW) wrote the conductivity in terms of a memory function M⁡(ω)M(\omega) as σ⁡(ω+i​η)=(i​n​e2/m)​(ω+M⁡(ω+i​η))−1\sigma(\omega+i\eta)=(ine^{2}/m)(\omega+M(\omega+i\eta))^{-1}, where M⁡(ω+i​η)=i/τM(\omega+i\eta)=i/\tau in the Drude limit. The analytic properties of −M⁡(ω+i​η)-M(\omega+i\eta) are the same as those of the self-energy Σ\Sigma of a retarded Green’s function. In the approximate treatment of GW, −M-M closely resembles a self-energy, with differences, e.g., the imaginary part is twice too large. The correct relation between −M-M and Σ\Sigma is known for the electron-phonon case and is conjectured to be similar for other perturbations. When vertex corrections are ignored there is a known relation. A derivation using Matsubara temperature Green’s functions is given.

I Preliminaries

Holstein [1] used elementary arguments to show that in the infrared properties of metals there can be quantum effects (outside of the semiclassical Boltzmann approach) when the temperature is low enough and the probing frequency ω\omega is degenerate with non-electronic excitations like phonons. Such effects have been seen experimentally [2, 3]. Götze and Wölfle (GW) [4] gave a nice simplified way to compute such effects in the optical response of metals using truncated equations of motion to compute the “memory function” M⁡(ω+i​η)M(\omega+i\eta) defined as

σ⁡(ω+i​η)=i​n​e2/mω+M⁡(ω+i​η).\sigma(\omega+i\eta)=\frac{ine^{2}/m}{\omega+M(\omega+i\eta)}. (1)

In the dc limit, their formulas correctly reproduce lowest-order variational solutions of the corresponding Boltzmann transport theories. Unfortunately, a systematic perturbation theory for M⁡(ω+i​η)M(\omega+i\eta) is not known, and the GW approximation is therefore hard to improve. The GW results are slightly less accurate than the corresponding lowest-order results of Green’s function theories.

The function −M⁡(ω+i​η)-M(\omega+i\eta) has causal analytic properties and, not surprisingly, bears a close resemblance to an electron self-energy Σ⁡(k→,ω+i​η)\Sigma(\vec{k},\omega+i\eta) for k→\vec{k}-points averaged over the Fermi surface. However, the imaginary part of Σ\Sigma is −1/2τ-1/2\tau while the imaginary part of −M-M must be −1/τ-1/\tau. This is not the only difference between −M-M and Σ\Sigma. Since the analogy between −M-M and Σ\Sigma is sometimes used for analysis of infrared spectra [5], it is important to understand just how good it actually is. A full formula seems not to have been derived, and is beyond the ambition of this paper. A reasonable conjecture is that when anisotropy with kk around the Fermi surface is not too important, then

σ⁡(ω+i​η)=i​n​e2m​ω​∫−∞∞d​ω′​f⁡(ω′)−f⁡(ω′+ω)ω−Σir​(ω′+ω+i​η)+Σir∗​(ω′+i​η),\sigma(\omega+i\eta)=\frac{ine^{2}}{m\omega}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}\frac{f(\omega^{\prime})-f(\omega^{\prime}+\omega)}{\omega-\Sigma_{\rm ir}(\omega^{\prime}+\omega+i\eta)+\Sigma_{\rm ir}^{\ast}(\omega^{\prime}+i\eta)}, (2)

where f⁡(ω′)=(exp⁡(β​ω′)+1)−1f(\omega^{\prime})=(\exp(\beta\omega^{\prime})+1)^{-1} is the Fermi-Dirac function. Here Σir\Sigma_{\rm ir} is a modified version of Σ\Sigma, averaged over the Fermi surface, but with an extra weighting factor, similar to the familiar transport factor 1−cos⁡θ1-\cos\theta. The actual weighting factor (in the solved electron-phonon case [6, 7]) is found from a frequency-dependent non-linear integral equation. Replacement of the weight factor by 1, turning Σir\Sigma_{\rm ir} into an ordinary, but k→\vec{k}-averaged, self-energy, should work fairly well in most cases. Scher [8] did a numerical study which tends to confirm that the difference between Σir\Sigma_{\rm ir} and Σ\Sigma is small. Sometimes the anisotropy of Σ\Sigma around the Fermi surface is large. A modified version of Eq.(2) that deals approximately with such cases is presented at the end of the paper.

Eq. (2) implies a relation between −M⁡(ω+i​η)-M(\omega+i\eta) and the self-energy which becomes more direct at low frequencies. Keeping the lowest order (in ω\omega) terms, one gets a derivative of the Fermi-Dirac function −∂f(ω′)/∂ω′-\partial f(\omega^{\prime})/\partial\omega^{\prime} which can be approximated by the Dirac δ⁡(ω′)\delta(\omega^{\prime}).

σ⁡(ω+i​η)\displaystyle\sigma(\omega+i\eta) ≈\displaystyle\approx i​n​e2m​∫−∞∞d​ω′​(−∂f⁡(ω′)∂ω′)\displaystyle\frac{ine^{2}}{m}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}\left(-\frac{\partial f(\omega^{\prime})}{\partial\omega^{\prime}}\right) (3)
×\displaystyle\times 1ω⁡(1−d​Σir,1​(ω′)/d​ω′)+2​i​Σir,2​(ω′)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\omega(1-d\Sigma_{{\rm ir},1}(\omega^{\prime})/d\omega^{\prime})+2i\Sigma_{{\rm ir},2}(\omega^{\prime})}
≈\displaystyle\approx i​n​e2/mω−ω​d​Σir,1​(ω)/d​ω+2​i​Σir,2​(ω)\displaystyle\frac{ine^{2}/m}{\omega-\omega d\Sigma_{{\rm ir},1}(\omega)/d\omega+2i\Sigma_{{\rm ir},2}(\omega)}

Therefore the real part of −M-M at low frequencies is ω​d​Re​Σir​(ω)/d​ω\omega d{\rm Re}\Sigma_{\rm ir}(\omega)/d\omega, and the imaginary part is −2​Im​Σir​(ω)-2{\rm Im}\Sigma_{\rm ir}(\omega). If the interesting part of Re​Σ{\rm Re}\Sigma is odd in ω\omega, and approximately linear, then MM at very low ω\omega is a lot like Σ\Sigma except for the factor of 2 in the imaginary part.

In the dc limit, the result σ=n​e2​τ/m\sigma=ne^{2}\tau/m is retrieved, with 1/τ=−2​Im​Σir​(ω→0)1/\tau=-2{\rm Im}\Sigma_{\rm ir}(\omega\rightarrow 0). There are minor differences between this and the more exact result found from a solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. These differences arise from k→\vec{k} dependence, and disappear when the electron scattering is isotropic.

II Kubo formula

The starting point is the Kubo [9] formula for the conductivity. In an external electric field E→​(t)=E→​cos⁡(ω​t)\vec{E}(t)=\vec{E}\cos(\omega t), the current operator j=−e∑kvk​xc†kckj=-e\sum_{k}v_{kx}c^{\dagger}_{k}c_{k} acquires an expectation value ⟨j⁡(t)⟩=Re⁡[σ⁡(ω+i​η)​exp⁡(−i​ω​t)]​E\langle j(t)\rangle={\rm Re}[\sigma(\omega+i\eta)\exp(-i\omega t)]E, where the linear response coefficient σ⁡(ω+i​η)\sigma(\omega+i\eta) is

σ⁡(ω+i​η)=iω​[r⁡(ω+i​η)+n​e2m]\sigma(\omega+i\eta)=\frac{i}{\omega}\left[r(\omega+i\eta)+\frac{ne^{2}}{m}\right] (4)
r⁡(ω+i​η)=i​∫0∞d​t​ei​ω​t−η​t​⟨[j⁡(t),j⁡(0)]⟩r(\omega+i\eta)=i\int_{0}^{\infty}dte^{i\omega t-\eta t}\langle[j(t),j(0)]\rangle (5)

The Hamiltonian ℋ=ℋ0+ℋ1{\cal H}={\cal H}_{0}+{\cal H}_{1} has the non-interacting part ℋ0=∑kϵk​ck†​ck{\cal H}_{0}=\sum_{k}\epsilon_{k}c^{\dagger}_{k}c_{k}. The label kk is short for the Bloch wavevector and other quantum numbers (k→​n​σ)(\vec{k}n\sigma). The state kk has energy ϵk\epsilon_{k} and group velocity v→k\vec{v}_{k}.

To obtain a Wick-ordered perturbation theory we use an imaginary time (0≤σ≤β=1/kB​T0\leq\sigma\leq\beta=1/k_{B}T) version of r⁡(ω)r(\omega),

r(iωμ)=−∫0βdσei​ωμ​σ⟨T^​j​(σ)​j​(0)⟩¯r(i\omega_{\mu})=-\int_{0}^{\beta}d\sigma e^{i\omega_{\mu}\sigma}\overline{\langle\hat{T}j(\sigma)j(0)\rangle} (6)

where j⁡(σ)=exp⁡(σ​ℋ)​j​exp⁡(−σ​ℋ)j(\sigma)=\exp(\sigma{\cal H})j\exp(-\sigma{\cal H}). Angular brackets denote a canonical ensemble temperature average, and the overbar indicates, if necessary, an average over an ensemble of randomly distributed impurities. The Matsubara frequency ωμ\omega_{\mu} is 2​π​μ/β2\pi\mu/\beta and μ\mu is an integer. When analytically continued from i​ωμi\omega_{\mu} to ω+i​η\omega+i\eta just above the real ω\omega axis (η\eta is a positive infinitesimal) r⁡(i​ωμ)r(i\omega_{\mu}) becomes r⁡(ω+i​η)r(\omega+i\eta), the retarded correlation function needed for the Kubo formula.

All Feynman graphs for r⁡(i​ωμ)r(i\omega_{\mu}) are formally summed in terms of the exact electron Green’s function

G⁡(k,i​ων)=1i​ων−ϵk−Σ⁡(k,i​ων),G(k,i\omega_{\nu})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{\nu}-\epsilon_{k}-\Sigma(k,i\omega_{\nu})}, (7)

and the exact vertex function Γ⁡(k,k′,i​ωμ,i​ων)\Gamma(k,k^{\prime},i\omega_{\mu},i\omega_{\nu}), where ων=2​π​(ν+1/2)/β\omega_{\nu}=2\pi(\nu+1/2)/\beta. The exact answer is

r⁡(i​ωμ)\displaystyle r(i\omega_{\mu}) =\displaystyle= −e2β∑k​k′​νvk′​xΓ(kk′,iωμ,iων)\displaystyle-\frac{e^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{kk^{\prime}\nu}v_{k^{\prime}x}\Gamma(kk^{\prime},i\omega_{\mu},i\omega_{\nu}) (8)
×\displaystyle\times G⁡(k′,i​ων+i​ωμ)​G​(k,i​ων)\displaystyle G(k^{\prime},i\omega_{\nu}+i\omega_{\mu})G(k,i\omega_{\nu})

Neither Σ\Sigma nor Γ\Gamma can be calculated exactly. A linearized Boltzmann equation is obtained when lowest-order results for Σ\Sigma and Γ\Gamma are treated consistently.

An explicit formula relating σ\sigma to Σ\Sigma occurs when Γ\Gamma is replaced by its lowest-order term,

Γ⁡(k​k′,i​ωμ,i​ων)→Γ0=vk​x​δ​(k,k′).\Gamma(kk^{\prime},i\omega_{\mu},i\omega_{\nu})\rightarrow\Gamma_{0}=v_{kx}\delta(k,k^{\prime}). (9)

The corresponding answer for σ⁡(ω+i​η)\sigma(\omega+i\eta), denoted by σ0​(ω+i​η)\sigma_{0}(\omega+i\eta), after continuing to the real frequency axis, and averaging away the k-dependence of Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta), is

σ0​(ω+i​η)=i​n​e2m​ω​∫−∞∞d​ω′​f⁡(ω′)−f⁡(ω′+ω)ω−Σ⁡(ω′+ω+i​η)+Σ∗​(ω′+i​η).\sigma_{0}(\omega+i\eta)=\frac{ine^{2}}{m\omega}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}\frac{f(\omega^{\prime})-f(\omega^{\prime}+\omega)}{\omega-\Sigma(\omega^{\prime}+\omega+i\eta)+\Sigma^{\ast}(\omega^{\prime}+i\eta)}. (10)

This is the desired approximation, a simplification of the conjectured version, Eq.(2). It is not particularly original. A derivation for a “local Fermi liquid” is given by Berthod et al. [10] It seems worthwhile to present a simpler and more general discussion. A careful derivation of Eq.(10) is given in the next section. This derivation has been available as an arXiv preprint since 2004. [11]

Unlike the conjectured version Eq. (2), the approximation of Eq. (9) does not correctly reproduce the Boltzmann dc conductivity because of the omission of vertex corrections. This is related to the fact that the quasiparticle scattering rate 1/τ=−2​Im​Σ1/\tau=-2{\rm Im}\Sigma differs from the transport scattering rate 1/τtr=−2​Im​Σir1/\tau_{\rm tr}=-2{\rm Im}\Sigma_{\rm ir} by a factor of the type 1−cos⁡θ1-\cos\theta. The “cos⁡θ\cos\theta” correction (omitted if the integral equation part of the Boltzmann equation is neglected) takes into account that small angle θ\theta scattering events (k→→k→′\vec{k}\rightarrow\vec{k}^{\prime}) do not degrade the current efficiently and make smaller contributions to 1/τtr1/\tau_{\rm tr} than to 1/τ1/\tau. The difference, except at low temperatures, is likely to be numerically small, since small angle scattering does not usually play a dominant role. The version of this applicable to electron-phonon-coupled superconductors was given by Nam. [12]

III Derivation of Eq. (10)

Starting by inserting Eq. (9) into Eq. (8),

r0(iωμ)=−e2β∑kvk​x2G(k,iων+iωμ)G(k,iων)r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu})=-\frac{e^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}G(k,i\omega_{\nu}+i\omega_{\mu})G(k,i\omega_{\nu}) (11)

This approximation, labeled r0r_{0}, keeps in principle arbitrarily complicated self-energy graphs in GG.

The spectral function is defined as

G⁡(k,i​ων)=∫−∞∞d​ω​A⁡(k,ω)i​ων−ωG(k,i\omega_{\nu})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega\frac{A(k,\omega)}{i\omega_{\nu}-\omega} (12)
A(k,ω)=−1πImG(k,iων→ω+iη)A(k,\omega)=-\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}G(k,i\omega_{\nu}\rightarrow\omega+i\eta) (13)

where G⁡(k,ω+i​η)G(k,\omega+i\eta) is the “retarded” Green’s function,

G⁡(k,ω+i​η)=1ω−ϵk−Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)G(k,\omega+i\eta)=\frac{1}{\omega-\epsilon_{k}-\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta)} (14)

and Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)=Δ⁡(k,ω)−i/2​τ​(k,ω)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta)=\Delta(k,\omega)-i/2\tau(k,\omega) has imaginary part 1/2​τ1/2\tau non-negative. The approximate correlation function r0r_{0} becomes

r0​(i​ωμ)\displaystyle r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu}) =\displaystyle= −e2β∑kvk​x2∫−∞∞dω1∫−∞∞dω2A(k,ω1)A(k,ω2)\displaystyle-\frac{e^{2}}{\beta}\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{2}A(k,\omega_{1})A(k,\omega_{2}) (15)
×\displaystyle\times ∑ν[1i​ων+i​ωμ−ω1​1i​ων−ω2]\displaystyle\sum_{\nu}\left[\frac{1}{i\omega_{\nu}+i\omega_{\mu}-\omega_{1}}\ \frac{1}{i\omega_{\nu}-\omega_{2}}\right]

The Matsubara sum can be performed exactly,

−1β∑ν[1i​ων+i​ωμ−ω11i​ων−ω2]=f⁡(ω2)−f⁡(ω1)ω2−ω1+i​ωμ.-\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{\nu}\left[\frac{1}{i\omega_{\nu}+i\omega_{\mu}-\omega_{1}}\ \frac{1}{i\omega_{\nu}-\omega_{2}}\right]=\frac{f(\omega_{2})-f(\omega_{1})}{\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}+i\omega_{\mu}}. (16)

The correlation function now is

r0(iωμ)=−e2∫−∞∞dϵ∑kvk​x2δ(ϵ−ϵk)∫−∞∞dω1\displaystyle r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu})=-e^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_{k})\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{1} (17)
×\displaystyle\times ∫−∞∞d​ω2​A​(k,ω1)​A​(k,ω2)​f⁡(ω2)−f⁡(ω1)ω2−ω1+i​ωμ,\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{2}A(k,\omega_{1})A(k,\omega_{2})\frac{f(\omega_{2})-f(\omega_{1})}{\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}+i\omega_{\mu}},

where a gratuitous factor 1=∫d​ϵ​δ​(ϵ−ϵk)1=\int d\epsilon\delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_{k}) was inserted. From Eqs.(13,14), the spectral function has a rapid ϵk\epsilon_{k}-dependence,

A⁡(k,ω)=−(1/π)​Im​[ω−ϵk−Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)]−1.A(k,\omega)=-(1/\pi){\rm Im}[\omega-\epsilon_{k}-\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta)]^{-1}. (18)

But because of the δ\delta function in the kk-sum

∑kvk​x2​δ​(ϵ−ϵk)​A​(k,ω1)​A​(k,ω2),\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_{k})A(k,\omega_{1})A(k,\omega_{2}), (19)

it is allowed to replace ϵk\epsilon_{k} in the denominators of the spectral functions by ϵ\epsilon. The rapid ϵ\epsilon-dependence in A⁡(k,ω)A(k,\omega) must be treated carefully, but the remaining weak kk dependence of Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta) in the denominator of A⁡(k,ω)A(k,\omega) can often be treated less carefully. For many metals, the self-energies Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta) in the spectral functions −(1/π)​Im​(ω−ϵ−Σ)−1-(1/\pi){\rm Im}(\omega-\epsilon-\Sigma)^{-1} vary weakly with k→\vec{k}, and can be replaced by their kk-average over the Fermi surface,

Σ⁡(ω+i​η)=∑kΣ⁡(k,ω+i​η)​δ​(ϵk)/∑kδ⁡(ϵk).\Sigma(\omega+i\eta)=\sum_{k}\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta)\delta(\epsilon_{k})/\sum_{k}\delta(\epsilon_{k}). (20)

In “conventional” s-wave superconductors, for example, anisotropy of the gap function Δ⁡(k,ω)\Delta(k,\omega) is often surprisingly small, and the gap can be approximated well as Δ⁡(ω)\Delta(\omega). The gap Δ⁡(k,ω)\Delta(k,\omega) is a superconducting extension of the normal state self energy. Serious anisotropy is not forbidden, and is known to occur in the TcT_{c}=39K superconductor MgB2 [13], for example. A modified formula applicable to such cases is given at the end of the paper. Using Eq.(20), the kk-sum is

∑kvk​x2​δ​(ϵ−ϵk)\displaystyle\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_{k}) =\displaystyle= 1ℏ2​∑k∂ϵk∂kx​(−∂f∂kx)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}}\sum_{k}\frac{\partial\epsilon_{k}}{\partial k_{x}}\left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial k_{x}}\right) (21)
=\displaystyle= 1ℏ2​∑k∂2ϵk∂kx2​f=[n/m]eff​(ϵ).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}}\sum_{k}\frac{\partial^{2}\epsilon_{k}}{\partial k_{x}^{2}}f=[n/m]_{\rm eff}(\epsilon).

Here the δ\delta function was replaced by −∂f/∂ϵk-\partial f/\partial\epsilon_{k}. An integration by parts was used to obtain the inverse effective mass (∂2ϵk/∂kx2)/ℏ2(\partial^{2}\epsilon_{k}/\partial k_{x}^{2})/\hbar^{2} summed over all states lower in energy than ϵ\epsilon.

The range of the remaining ϵ\epsilon-integration is nominally (−∞,∞)(-\infty,\infty). However, the factors A⁡(k,ω)A(k,\omega) are peaked at ϵ≈ω1\epsilon\approx\omega_{1} and ϵ≈ω2\epsilon\approx\omega_{2}. Thus the integrand is large only if ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2} have similar values. Because of the factor (f⁡(ω2)−f⁡(ω1))(f(\omega_{2})-f(\omega_{1})), they must both lie near the Fermi energy (one below and one above.) Therefore the ϵ\epsilon integral is dominated by ϵ\epsilon near the Fermi energy. The value of [n/m]eff​(ϵ)[n/m]_{\rm eff}(\epsilon) at the Fermi energy is [n/m]eff[n/m]_{\rm eff}, the number of electrons divided by the effective mass averaged over all states below the Fermi energy. An equivalent formula is

[n/m]eff=∑kvk​x2​δ​(ϵk)=N⁡(0)<vx2>[n/m]_{\rm eff}=\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon_{k})=N(0)<v_{x}^{2}> (22)

The current correlation function now is

r0​(i​ωμ)\displaystyle r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu}) =\displaystyle= [nm]eff​e2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​∫−∞∞d​ω1​∫−∞∞d​ω2\displaystyle\left[\frac{n}{m}\right]_{\rm eff}e^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{2} (23)
×\displaystyle\times A⁡(ϵ,ω1)​A​(ϵ,ω2)​f⁡(ω2)−f⁡(ω1)ω2−ω1+i​ωμ.\displaystyle A(\epsilon,\omega_{1})A(\epsilon,\omega_{2})\frac{f(\omega_{2})-f(\omega_{1})}{\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}+i\omega_{\mu}}.

It is necessary to integrate ϵ\epsilon carefully over the Lorentzian peaks of A⁡(ϵ,ω1)​A​(ϵ,ω2)A(\epsilon,\omega_{1})A(\epsilon,\omega_{2}). Cauchy’s theorem can be used after closing the ϵ\epsilon-contour by an arc going to infinity in either the upper or lower half-plane. The result is expressed by another identity,

∫−∞∞𝑑ϵ\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon (1π)​Im​(1ω1−ϵ−Σ1)​(1π)​Im​(1ω2−ϵ−Σ2)\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\right){\rm Im}\left(\frac{1}{\omega_{1}-\epsilon-\Sigma_{1}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\right){\rm Im}\left(\frac{1}{\omega_{2}-\epsilon-\Sigma_{2}}\right) (24)
=\displaystyle= −(1π)​Im​(1ω1−ω2−Σ1+Σ2∗).\displaystyle-\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\right){\rm Im}\left(\frac{1}{\omega_{1}-\omega_{2}-\Sigma_{1}+\Sigma_{2}^{\ast}}\right).

The proof is elementary but tedious. The current correlation function is now

r0​(i​ωμ)\displaystyle r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu}) =\displaystyle= [nm]eff​e2π​∫−∞∞d​ω1​∫−∞∞d​ω2​f⁡(ω2)−f⁡(ω1)ω2−ω1+i​ωμ\displaystyle\left[\frac{n}{m}\right]_{\rm eff}\frac{e^{2}}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega_{2}\frac{f(\omega_{2})-f(\omega_{1})}{\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}+i\omega_{\mu}} (25)

The function r0​(ω+i​η)r_{0}(\omega+i\eta) is now just r0​(i​ωμ)r_{0}(i\omega_{\mu}) with i​ωμi\omega_{\mu} replaced by ω+i​η\omega+i\eta. The only complex quantity in the formula for r0​(ω+i​η)r_{0}(\omega+i\eta) is the factor (ω2−ω1+ω+i​η)−1(\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}+\omega+i\eta)^{-1}, so the real part Re​σ0​(ω+i​η)=Im​r0​(ω+i​η)/ω{\rm Re}\sigma_{0}(\omega+i\eta)={\rm Im}r_{0}(\omega+i\eta)/\omega (Eq.(4)) is

=\displaystyle= [nm]eff​e2​∫−∞∞d​ω′​[f⁡(ω′)−f⁡(ω′+ω)ω]\displaystyle\left[\frac{n}{m}\right]_{\rm eff}e^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}\left[\frac{f(\omega^{\prime})-f(\omega^{\prime}+\omega)}{\omega}\right]

The function σ0​(ω+i​η)\sigma_{0}(\omega+i\eta) is specified by the requirements of being analytic for Im​ω>0{\rm Im}\omega>0, vanishing sufficiently rapidly as ω→∞\omega\rightarrow\infty, and agreeing with Eq. (26). It is necessary and sufficient to remove the “real part” designator from both sides. This is the derivation of Eq. (10).

Here is a modification of Eq.(10) that doesn’t ignore anisotropy of Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta) as k→\vec{k} varies around the Fermi surface.

σ0​(ω+i​η)=i​e2ω​∫−∞∞d​ω′​[f⁡(ω′)−f⁡(ω′+ω)]\displaystyle\sigma_{0}(\omega+i\eta)=\frac{ie^{2}}{\omega}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}[f(\omega^{\prime})-f(\omega^{\prime}+\omega)] (27)
×\displaystyle\times ∑kvk​x2​δ​(ϵk−ϵF)ω−Σ⁡(k,ω′+ω+i​η)+Σ∗​(k,ω′+i​η)\displaystyle\sum_{k}\frac{v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{F})}{\omega-\Sigma(k,\omega^{\prime}+\omega+i\eta)+\Sigma^{\ast}(k,\omega^{\prime}+i\eta)}

To derive this, go back to Eq.(17) but do not use the isotropic form Eq.(20) for Σ\Sigma, and do not make use of Eq.(21). The factor [n/m]eff[n/m]_{\rm eff} no longer appears outside the integrals, but ∑kvk​x2​δ​(ϵk−ϵ)\sum_{k}v_{kx}^{2}\delta(\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon) appears inside the d​ϵd\epsilon integral in Eq.(23). It is no longer possible to use Eq.(24), unless an approximation is made, namely that the k→\vec{k}-dependence of vk​x2v_{kx}^{2} and of Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta) is not too rapid. There can be a large variation of both vk​x2v_{kx}^{2} and Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta) as k→\vec{k} moves around the Fermi surface. However, the variation perpendicular to the Fermi surface, as ϵk\epsilon_{k} changes on the scale of the relevant infrared ω\omega’s, must be small. Then one can ignore the ϵ\epsilon-dependence of both vk​x2v_{kx}^{2} and Σ⁡(k,ω+i​η)\Sigma(k,\omega+i\eta), and recover the use of Eq.(24). Then Eq.(27) follows. A version of this approximation was used by Hussey et al. [14] for analysis of the normal state of cuprates.
